In summary, our research is concerned with

the characterization of NS3/4 protease quasispecie diversity of AHC patients co‐infected with HIV, which is a growing problem in the last decade, as well as the identification of epidemiological networks in HIV‐1‐coinfected men who have sex.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

AHC HIV‐1‐coinfected MSM patients have a high NS3/4a protease efficiency, a high viral diversity, a high ds/dn ratio and a high rate of HCV transmission, all of which may be associated with a poor virological response to treatment.
HCV NS3 quasispecies in HIV‐1‐co‐infected MSM with AHC exhibit higher genetic diversity and NS3 protease catalytic efficiency than in HIV‐1 monoinfected MSM with ACH.
NS3/4a protease efficiency may play a role in HCV infection and treatment outcome.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the NS3/4 proteases from ACH patients are more efficient in cleaving MAVS than the NS3/ 4 proteases from CHC patients.

HCV NS3‐4A quasispeces in AHC patients with HIV‐1 coinfection are characterized by high diversity and efficiency in the cleavage of MAVS, a marker of interferon sensitivity, which may contribute to viral persistence in the absence of therapy and to the response to pegIFNs in the presence of therapy.
the NS3/4 protease of HCV is highly variable and the catalytic efficiency is higher in acute infection than in chronic infection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the NS3/4 protease of AHC patients is more efficient in cleaving MAVS than that of patients with CHC.
HCV quasispecies diversity is higher in HIV‐coinfeced MSM with AHC compared to CHC.
